author: petrikrohn_26497
message: For the clean room:  ## A cryptography question: Suppose you had a numbered set of AES-128-ECB keys in the form of - `0123456789...0123456789XX`  where `0123456789`... would be a common hex string shared by all keys and `XX` the number of the key in hex form. For the Rijndael encryption, you need to split the 16-byte key into four 4-byte words to be used as round keys rk[0], rk[1], rk[2], and rk[3]. The algorithm first uses rk[0] and then the others in sequence. This way rk[0] produces most entropy.  Would it therefore be safer to reverse the order of the 4-byte words and use the last 8 hex characters of the humanly readable key as rk[0] instead of rk[3]? Should Nvidia also be doing the same if they use similar keys for their numbered keys?  Using a common part for the numbered keys would save a lot of fuses. 30 fuses vs 256 x 32 fuses.

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: ## Subtasks There are three separate things that need to be done to recreate the previous proof-of-concept. - Modify the Nvidia open source drivers so that they pass an oversized fake signature exploit to the GPU. The driver then needs to modify the registers via BAR0. - Create an exploit that modifies the PLMs so that the registers become host-writable. This is a ROP chain based on the cleartext booter code. - Find Nvidia's non-secret obfuscation key for debug code. This allows decrypting the debug version of the booter. The production version is exactly the same.

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: I think there was a misunderstanding.  The GPU die has two device IDs fused into it, one named `ORIGNAL` and the other named `REBRAND`. (This is described in an Nvidia patent.) There is a strap resistor `strap5` that changes between the two.  On the 170HX 10GB die the values are fused to `2082` and `20C2`. On the 8GB version they are both `20C2`. I have not been able to locate the resistor, although I have found the five others.  The VBIOS cannot change the device ID of the card. The alternate device ID on VBIOS likely only means that the VBIOS will run on a card with that ID.

message: No. The encrypted part starts at` 0x100`. (a multiple of 16) You need to splice together the two parts. - First `0x100` bytes as is. - Rest decrypted  To disassemble, make sure that there are an even number of zero padding bytes around `0xFF`. If you get something like this, it is gibberish (This is from booter 515) ` 000000f9: 3e f9 00 00         B lbra 0xf9 000000fd: 00 00                 mov $r0 0x0 000000ff: 00 89                 mov $r0 -0x77 00000101: fc ff                 ??? $r15 [unknown: 00 0f] [unknown instruction] 00000103: 00 fe                 mov $r0 -0x2 00000105: 94 00 f5              shl b32 $r0 $r0 0xf5 00000108: 3c 00 e0              add b8 $r14 $r0 $r0`  The first instruction of the encrypted part at `0x100` is: `89 fc ff 00           mov $r9 0xfffc`

Ignore it! ### A quick look at the gadget list:  The most important gadget is this: `GADGET_BAR0_WRITE  = 0x0F40` As the name says, it writes a value we control to the desired register in the 32-bit BAR0 address space.  The address of the gadget is `0x0F40`, which contains this long section of code. The function this is part of starts at `0x0f39`, so only the fist two instructions are missing. ` 00000f40: f9 22                 mpush $r2 00000f42: bf ff                 ld b32 $r15 D[$r15] 00000f44: fe 49 01              mov $r9 $sp 00000f47: b2 a2                 mov b32 $r2 $r10 00000f49: 90 99 0c              add b32 $r9 $r9 0xc 00000f4c: a0 9f                 st b32 D[$r9] $r15 00000f4e: 4a 00 0c            B mov $r10 0xc00 00000f51: 7e 64 82 00           lcall 0x8264 00000f55: b2 a0                 mov b32 $r0 $r10 00000f57: 4a 00 0b              mov $r10 0xb00 00000f5a: 7e 64 82 00           lcall 0x8264  00000f67: a6 0a                 cmp b32 $r0 $r10 00000f69: f4 1b e5              bra ne 0xf4e 00000f6c: fe 49 01              mov $r9 $sp 00000f6f: 90 99 0c              add b32 $r9 $r9 0xc 00000f72: b5 20 01              st b32 D[$r2+0x4] $r0 00000f75: a0 21                 st b32 D[$r2] $r1 00000f77: bf 9f                 ld b32 $r15 D[$r9] 00000f79: 89 40 63 00           mov $r9 0x6340 00000f7d: bf 99                 ld b32 $r9 D[$r9] 00000f7f: a6 f9                 cmp b32 $r15 $r9 00000f81: f4 0b 07              bra e 0xf88 00000f84: 7e d9 7d 00           lcall 0x7dd9 00000f88: fb 25 04            B mpopaddret $r2 0x4`  To use the gadget, you need to store the new value and its address in BAR0 in two of the 16 registers. message: To use the `BAR0Write($r10, $r11)` function we need to be able to set registers `$r10` and `$r11`. author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```   Through systematic isolation (all FLR-verified, fires isolated):   - Every write-variant fails 0xccb → finalize=0x01000000; whole_stack (no write) passes → 0x11000000.   - Ruled out: BCR-specific (scratch write fails identically), shared-BAR0M state (different reg block), main-SP frame collision at 0x10, and overflow size (0xF810 fails identically).   - Root cause pinned: the write's inherent +0x18 main-SP shift puts main at 0xFFFC; 0xccb's SP-relative accesses then wrap past 0x10000. whole_stack keeps main at 0xFFE4 (no wrap) → passes. Constraint: main must be < 0xFFF0 (shift ≤ ~0xB), but the   minimum BAR0-master write is +0x10 (full-0x10aa) / +0x18 (0x10b9).    The block    Getting main back under 0xFFF0 needs SP compensation, and the booter has no clean SP-lowering gadget — mov $sp $r9 exists only at _start (re-runs boot), and all mpush/add $sp -N are inside function prologues. This is a genuine gadget-availability   constraint.```

author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```Bumping this to 0xF810 makes the DMA wrap into DMEM 0x0-0xF, so the shifted finalize locals (which land at 0x4/0x8 after the +0x18) become payload-controllable   — closing the exact gap that hung the SEC2 booter.```

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: ## Clanker's 3 ROP chains explained I have spent the last two hours studying the three ROP chains posted by Big Ptoughneigh yesterday. This is Big's bot Clanker explaining them in his own words. > ①  is the authentication vehicle (proven). ③ is the write engine (proven). ② is the attempted fusion — and the whole write-after-auth work is about fusing ① + ③ without the shift landing during the auth.  The chain ① `whole_stack_rejoin [0x37b7]` does nothing. It is used to verify the successful deployment of the exploit. The payload contains a copy of the reconstructed stack contents with the stack canaries replaced with our "fake bird" values. It is a pity that Clanker refused to provide a copy of the stack contents, despite it obviously knowing everything. The payload starts with the "WprMeta" at `0xFF3C`-`0xFF4C`. Wonder what WprMeta is and where Clanker found it.  ROP chain ③ `full_0x10aa` uses `0x10aa  reg_write_indirect` to write to BAR0. For an unknown reason it uses the 1fb9 → 1fbd elevator to move the BAR0 address and value from `$r0` to `$r10` and `$r11` and even uses a a totally unneeded `mpopaddret $r2 0x4` at `1fca` in between — instead of simply returning to `10b9` with the values in `$r1` and `$r2`. The chain terminates in PANIC. Are the canaries wrong, or did Clanker simply decide to call `7dd9`? Likely there was no stack space for anything else.  ROP chain ② `success_rejoin_write_v2 [0x37cc + BCR write]` — "most advanced, reaches finalize WITH the write"  The chain is simple and direct: `4d4` returns to `10b9` (`reg_write_indirect`) and rejoins `0x3747  image_copy_verify` at `37cc`. In other words, it simply adds `10b9 reg_write_indirect` to the middle of the stack, elongating it by 20 bytes. Problem is, this extends the stack past the bottom address `FFFF`. Evidently it is possible for the stack to wrap around to `0x0000`. This is what Clanker calls the the "enlarge-overflow trick (`0xF810`)", the last number being the new length of the payload.

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: The A100 40GB and the 170HX 10GB share the same strap resistor positions **LLLLH**. The memory straps must be **HLL** for strap 4 for Samsung 8GB stacks.  The five straps from left to right:  - Strap1 (R986, R987) `RAMCFG[1]` - Strap0 (R989, R990) `RAMCFG[0]` - Strap3 (R993, R994) `VGA_DEVICE` - Strap4 (R999, R1000) `PCIE_CFG` - Strap2 (R1004, R1005) `RAMCFG[2]`  The 170HX 8GB has Hynix 16GB dies and is strapped **HHLLH**, like it should be for strap 7 (Hynix 16GB HBM2e).

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: On GA100 cards, ECC is a feature of the HBM2 stack. On the 170HX, ECC is fused off can likely not be enabled.  If you look at the values for `Per-FBPA CSTATUS_RAMAMOUNT` an each of the enabled FBPAs, you will see something interesting. - On 170HX cards with memory limited to 2GB per stack the value is `0x0200`. On unlocked cards it is `0x0800 `or `0x1000` for 8GB and 16GB stacks. - On A100 cards, the values are `0x07ff` or `0x0fff` for 8GB and 16GB stacks. A small part of the stack is reserved for ECC. You will see the same weird numbers listed on TechPowerUp for the A100 .roms.  https://gist.github.com/JRex286/0480d2b2b35ad594e57b6543952be307

author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```GSP-RM is logging — decisive. GSP-LOG[INIT]: put=0x44 (68 bytes), GSP-LOG[INTR]: put=0x94 (148 bytes). So GSP-RM booted, wrote to its INIT log, and ran its    interrupt task — it's alive and executing, not silent. The earlier "empty log" was a decode failure (release firmware strips the format-string DB, so   kgspDumpGspLogs can't render the packed records), not GSP-RM producing nothing.    On your mailbox question — good instinct, and the answer clarifies the whole picture:      The GSP falcon MAILBOX0 (0x110040, NV_PFALCON_FALCON_MAILBOX0) is a plain 32-bit register, not a FIFO — reading it is non-destructive (returns the current   value, doesn't pop/clear). So our polling loop can't consume values or perturb the handshake; only a write could, and the watcher only reads. The values we saw   are the true register state at each moment: boot-args-PA → 0x80000000.      But your queue intuition is exactly right — it just applies to a different structure. The real queue is the RPC message ring in sysmem (msgqRx/Tx), which is a   FIFO the driver drains on read. GSP_INIT_DONE arrives on that ring, not via the mailbox. And 0x31 earlier wasn't a queue artifact — it was a written value (the   driver's boot-args PA, clobbered), read non-destructively. ```

message: In what order are the registers pushed and popped on the stack?

author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```The agents are digging into the 0x8119 context fix and msgqRxLink in the background. On your question — this is exactly the value-threading subtlety we nailed   down empirically on silicon (STATE.md §3f), so here's the precise order:    Falcon stack grows downward (SP decreases on push). For a multi-register block:           Push (mpush $rN) — pushes r0 first, ascending register number to rN last:   higher addr ──►  r0   (pushed first, highest address)                    r1                       ...   lower addr  ──►  rN   (pushed last, lowest address — SP points here)      Pop (mpop $rN / mpopaddret) — strict LIFO, so it's the reverse: rN comes off first (from the SP/lowest slot), r0 comes off last (from the highest slot). The   resulting register→slot mapping is:   r0  ← HIGHEST address in the popped block   r1  ← highest − 4   ...   rN  ← LOWEST address  (where SP points)      So the load-bearing rule for building payloads: r0 maps to the highest popped slot, not the lowest — the highest-numbered register sits at the bottom (SP), r0   at the top. That's the bug that bit us before: the emulator had r10 two words too low, and the silicon sweep showed r10's real slot was +8 (r0-at-highest   ordering). To feed a value into rK in a block whose top is address T, you write it at T − 4·K.      Why this matters for 0x8119 right now: the epilogue's mpopaddret $r0 0x10 unwinds relative to the current $sp — so if $sp isn't main's frame, not only is the   canary slot D[$sp+0x10] wrong, the register block it restores comes off the wrong addresses entirely (r0 from the wrong top). That's the second half of why my   0xFFD4 placement diverges, and it's what the disasm agent is pinning down so the frame/$sp and this pop-ordering line up. I'll fold its answer together with   this ordering when it reports back. ```

message: ```Card healthy (10240 MiB, 51°C), and confirmed — the installed driver is the proprietary blob (license: NVIDIA). Let me answer your question, then write the full   state doc.    Your question: which driver at each load?           Both loads run the same proprietary blob (/lib/modules/.../dkms/nvidia.ko, license NVIDIA) — it is not an open/proprietary split. The split is by mode, not by   driver:      - Load 0 — GSP-mode exploit fire (modprobe nvidia, CPU-RM config parked): proprietary blob, GSP mode, loading the patched gsp_tu10x.bin. The exploit lives in   the firmware .bin (not the driver), so the SEC2 booter fires the community chain here → lands LMR/strap/compute → clean exit → driver proceeds to a GSP-RM boot   that fails 0x62 (but writes landed + exit was clean).   - Load 1 — CPU-RM read (modprobe nvidia NVreg_EnableGpuFirmware=0): the same proprietary blob, CPU-RM/monolithic mode. This is where it reads LMR 0x100CE0 for   the reported size — and where the 0x24→0x25 walls are.      The critical consequence: the CPU-RM read (load 1) is proprietary and therefore unpatchable — I can't demote kbusVerifyBar2 or the StateLoad check in source.   Load 0 could be the open driver (it only needs to run the booter), but load 1 must be proprietary because the open driver is GSP-only on GA100 (insmod with   EnableGpuFirmware=0 → 0x62 firmware-init fail). So the only patchable driver that can report a size is the open driver in GSP mode with memmgr-force — which is   the rejoin/0xFFFF path, not CPU-RM.```

author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```Both strap and LMR must be unlocked to pass kbusVerifyBar2 and reach StateLoad. The LMR alone or strap alone fails one step earlier. So there's no version of   "reach StateLoad without the LMR" — the LMR is a hard prerequisite for even getting to 0x25.      What this tells us about 0x25        Combining everything measured today, 0x25 StateLoad:   - is reached only when strap and LMR are both above the fuse,   - is size-invariant (20/40/80 GB identical) → not a scrubber/ECC/capacity operation,   - survives RMDisableFastScrubber and a GSP engine reset.      That's the signature of a structural fuse-vs-geometry consistency check in the FB/memory-system StateLoad — it trips the instant the programmed geometry exceeds   the 10 GB fuse cap, regardless of by how much. Since the CPU-RM driver is the proprietary blob, that check can't be demoted in source on this path.    ```

author: bigptoughneigh
message: Clanking: The mbox PLM is one of a whole set the aborted booter raised. When I did exactly the HS-unlock approach on the reset-PLM (0x8403C4), it worked — SEC2’s kflcnReset came alive (CPUCTL 0x10→0x00) and the fresh booter actually ran. But it then faulted at 0x65 on the other still-raised PLMs (0x840470, 0x84052C, and cross-aperture ones). So unlocking the mbox PLM too just clears one more of many — the fresh booter still faults elsewhere and writes its own non-zero code, overwriting any value we planted.  And that’s the real bind, spelled out by the two branches:      •    Fresh booter runs (PLMs cleared enough) → it overwrites our mailbox with its result. To get 0 we need it to genuinely succeed, which needs the complete PLM set restored — the part my FIX-v3 found impractical.     •    Fresh booter can’t run (SEC2 frozen) → our planted mailbox 0 survives and passes the check → but GSP-RM was never loaded (our ROP ate the booter run that loads it) → stalls waiting for a GSP-RM that isn’t there.

message: I just noticed that `secure_teardown()` always exits before returning to `main()`. This means that there is no need to retain the `main() `or `start()` stack frames on the stack or in the payload.  This gives us 7 more words on the stack to play around with. More than enough for one more BAR0 write. ` // ============================================================================ // 0x7e76  secure_teardown //   Secure teardown before handing control on. Enable the 0x10100 DMA aperture, set //   $cauth|0x80000, wipe all SCP key regs $c0-$c7 (csecret+cxor=0), zero all 64KB of //   DMEM, clear GPRs, and `exit` (halt). Leaves no secrets in Falcon state. // ============================================================================ 00007e76: 8f 40 63 00        C  mov $r15 0x6340 ... 00007f63: bd e4                 clear b32 $r14 00007f65: bd f4                 clear b32 $r15 00007f67: f8 02                 exit 00007f69: fe 49 01              mov $r9 $sp 00007f6c: bf 9f                 ld b32 $r15 D[$r9] 00007f6e: 89 40 63 00           mov $r9 0x6340 00007f72: bf 99                 ld b32 $r9 D[$r9] 00007f74: a6 f9                 cmp b32 $r15 $r9 00007f76: f4 0b 07              bra e 0x7f7d 00007f79: 7e d9 7d 00           lcall 0x7dd9  // __stack_chk_fail 00007f7d: f4 30 04            B add $sp 0x4 00007f80: f8 00                 ret`  Exit is what is needed for the Falcon to exit HS mode and allow new code to be loaded.  (The canary check that you see at the end is just an artifact of the compiler.)

author: rubbra_f
message: this is what clancker said That line is a BAR0 register write in the ROP chain: Python (0x00840040, 0x00000000),  # 6. SEC2 clear   @ 0xFFC0 It means: write the value 0x00000000 to the register at BAR0 offset 0x00840040. What is 0x00840040? This is the SEC2 mailbox/status register on the GA100. SEC2 is the Security Engine 2 (a Falcon microprocessor) that handles the GSP secure boot sequence. During normal boot, this register holds status codes: 0x00 = success / idle 0x31 = incomplete / still processing (what you saw in your failed runs) Does it free resources? No — it does not free WPR2 or release memory. It only clears a status flag. What it does: Resets the SEC2 status to 0x00 (success/idle) Tells the RM/driver that the secure boot phase completed cleanly Prevents the driver from seeing the 0x31 ("incomplete") error and aborting The actual WPR2 release (freeing the write-protected region) is handled by the tail gadget at 0xFFC0 → 0x000027fa (booter_load_wpr_main), not by this BAR0 write. Why include it? In your earlier runs, SEC2 was stuck at 0x31 even though the other registers changed. By forcing it to 0x00, you prevent the driver from rejecting the card during RmInitAdapter due to a stale security error. It is a "clean-up" write to make the GPU state look legitimate after the exploit.

author: bigptoughneigh
message: The overflow is a static payload baked into the firmware signature, but the WPR2 layout it must reconstruct is dynamic (re-randomized each boot). The live inject is the bridge: it patches the current boot's real WprMeta values into that static payload at load time, so the reconstructed booter frame is consistent with where the GSP firmware actually landed. Without it, the booter finalizes against the wrong memory map (0xf0000000); with it, the map is correct (0x11000000) and GSP-RM comes up — which is exactly why this was the change that finally got it booting.

"Major device number 236" is just a dynamically-allocated Linux char-device major (alloc_chrdev_region grabs whatever's free from the kernel pool) — not hardware-derived, and it can differ per boot. It's logged at the lowest severity (DBG_INFO), the success-path "I'm loading" notice that prints on essentially every driver load.  The key distinction for our card: this is the NVLink software subsystem initializing (always happens, any GPU), not actual NVLink links training. On the CMP 170HX, NVLink is fused off (pcie-unlock-status.md: "NVLink+ECC+PCIe Gen2 ALL dead"), so the software layer loads exactly as printed but there's no functional fabric behind it. And it runs during early module load, before GPU/GSP bring-up — so it's not a signal about our boot progress either way. Safe to ignore.```  Pretty sure the clanker is just wrong on the hardware not being there. I'm not sure if the snippet actually made something new happen that doesn't normally happen though.

author: bigptoughneigh
message: The booter’s image_dma_loader (0x21f4) copies the entire radix3 — task_init text included — from sysmem into FB WPR2, page-by-page through DMEM 0x800, at call site 0x2725. That runs to completion before the signature DMA at 0x37b3 where our overflow fires, so the ROP can’t precede or skip it. The clincher: image_auth MACs the whole image read back from FB and passes — which is only possible if every page (including file offset 0x14000) is physically present in WPR2.  So the task pages are in FB. The PC=0 is confirmed to be a pure mapping problem — the GSP RISC-V MPU/page tables resolve task_init’s VA to physical 0 at first launch, even though the bytes are sitting right there. That’s exactly what the MPU-mapping fork is tracing from the RISC-V side, and what the hardware probe’s ICD read (mcause/mepc) would confirm directly.

author: bigptoughneigh
message: MPU fork found a specific, real fetch→PA0 mechanism: the bootstrap SMPU only maps the resident kernel (VA [0x4000000,0x4013000), region 3); task_init’s VA 0x4018000 is covered only by a region-8 identity map (VA0→PA0) unless the runtime pager (0x400b3c8) installs a real entry before the first mret. If it doesn’t, task_init fetches from unbacked PA 0x4018000 → 0. Base-PA source is a self-locating auipc delta at global 0x4002080 — which is why the resident always works.     •    Hardware fork says that never triggers — GSP-RM ran far enough to emit GSP_RUN_CPU_SEQUENCER and the stall is the mailbox0 handshake, making riscvPc=0 a host-lock artifact.

author: bigptoughneigh
message: The GA100 GSP boot inherently requires a second, SEC2-driven reload after task_rm‘s early init: GSP-RM does initial setup, asks the CPU to reset it and reload a resume shim, and then hand back through SEC2. Our single-shot exploit hijacks the first SEC2 load — but the boot demands a clean second SEC2 resume, and the exploited SEC2 state can’t provide it. On top of that, GSP-RM never even reaches the clean self-suspend (0x110040 stays 0).

author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```The self-suspend agent found the suspend write (MAILBOX0 |= 0x80000000 at 0x400a24c) and — critically — proved GSP-RM is alive, not crashed: falconMailbox0=0x31 is a live status write, no panic, and its newest LibOS logs are device-init memory-map work. It stalls inside RmInitNvDevice before it ever reaches the suspend syscall. And forcing the suspend is a dead end — if GSP suspended, it'd just be halted with no path to GSP_INIT_DONE, because the reload it's asking for is the SEC2 CORE_RESUME the exploit can't service.  Put together with the variant-G result: the GA100 GSP boot architecturally requires a mid-boot GSP reset + SEC2-driven reload, and our single-shot booter-overflow fundamentally can't provide a clean second SEC2 load (PLM-locked / wiped SCP context / no bit-26 code path).```

author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```So resetting the GSP into RISC-V from the intact, already-authenticated WPR2 does not self-relaunch it. SEC2's CORE_RESUME isn't just the bit-26 doorbell — it performs the actual HS-authenticated RISC-V reload. The GA100 GSP boot requires a clean mid-boot SEC2-driven reset+reload during device-init, and our booter-overflow destroys SEC2's ability to do it (PLM-locked, SCP keys wiped, no bit-26 code path).  The HS-write needs the SEC2 booter exploit; the boot needs a clean SEC2 mid-boot reload; the exploit breaks exactly what the boot needs. Variant-G (0x1180f8) is trivially settable but doesn't help, because SEC2 still can't resume.  ```

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: ## 96GB on every card, but unusable Every 170HX and A100 card we have seen so far, has all six HBM2 stacks present and working. (96GB for the 8GB model).  There are two FBPs for each HBM2 stack. Each FBP is further divided into two FBPAs. The FBPs are disabled by one-time programmable OPT fuses. On every card we have seen, the disabled FBPs are on different stacks, meaning some of the stacks are working in 512-bit wide mode, but every one is at least partly working.  On a typical 8GB card, you would see 2 FBPs marked as defective and a further 2 FBPs marked as disabled, leaving 8 active FBPs across six stacks.  I suggested yesterday in a private chat (yes private, not to distract Clanker from the work he should actually be doing) that it might be possible to enable more VRAM by setting LMR to a higher value than what the CFG1 strap would suggest or allow.  GMZombie007's strap experiment showed a strange behavior, where the low LMR value limited the card to only one working stack. I speculated, that an oversize LMR might enable more stacks. I will share below a conversation I had about issue. The first post is the OPT fuses from a 170HX card. The second one is my analysis of it.

message: from the clanker: ```Right — for the boot/devinit path, which is exactly what the two-load uses. This is the reconciliation of two things that looked contradictory:  At boot: setting the broadcast 0x9A0204 → devinit reads it and programs every FBPA's per-FBPA CFG1 itself. Our STEP 2 confirmed this on hardware — load1 set only the broadcast, and load2's devinit trained all the FBPAs (CSTATUS 0x200→0x800). So no individual writes needed. Their intuition is correct. At runtime (driverless, no devinit): the broadcast alone does not move CSTATUS — that's why our earlier driverless work had to write all 20 per-FBPA CFG1 by hand. No devinit was running to propagate the broadcast. So both are true in their own context, and their point actually validates our current load1 (which sets only the broadcast). Good simplification.  Their "unless you can enable disabled FBPs for more VRAM" caveat — no, and we've fuse-proven it. The disabled FBPs (FBP6, FBP11) are FBP_DEFECTIVE = 0x840 = genuinely dead silicon, with STATUS_HALF_FBPA = 0 (no recoverable half-cap fuses) and DISABLE == DEFECTIVE (nothing merely binned-off). So they can't be re-enabled — 80 GB is the ceiling for our card, not 96.  Net: their model is accurate, and reassuringly it matches exactly what the worker is doing on STEP 3 right now (broadcast strap in load1 + the 0xff-clean-exit lever + .04 patched load2). author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```A clean SEC2 exit and 0x8403C4 = 0x8f are the same action. The 0x8f isn't stale state left lying around that we can overwrite — it's stamped by the booter's own clean-exit teardown (the priv-lockdown), which runs after anything our ROP does. So:  Host-write it after the fire: fails — once it's 0x8f, 0x8403C4 self-seals to read-only below PL0; every value we write (0xff/0xffffffff/0xdf) is ignored. The host can lower protection but can't raise 0x8f back to 0xff. Embed an HS-write in the ROP before the exit: fails two ways — the teardown re-stamps 0x8f after our write, and empirically touching the reset-PLM mid-HS hung the GSP boot (the identical fire without that one write completes fine). So there's genuinely no ordering where SEC2 exits clean and leaves 0x8403C4 ≠ 0x8f: run the teardown → 0x8f blocks load2; skip the teardown → SEC2 frozen-in-HS, load2 rejected anyway. author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```1. "v2's mutex-clear" / the ACR mutex. Honest answer: I don't have a "v2 mutex-clear" step in my current working notes — it's likely from earlier context, and the _v2.asm above is the v2 annotated booter disasm, so "v2's mutex-clear" probably refers to a mutex-release the v2 analysis spotted in that booter. The mechanism itself is real and matters: the booter is HS ucode that acquires a Falcon hardware mutex before touching WPR/ACR (read MUTEX_ID → get a handle → write it into a MUTEX(i) register; release = write IDLE/0). Its purpose is to serialize ACR/WPR access. If our exploit's HS code acquired a mutex and its abnormal HS exit never released it, load2's booter's acquire fails/branches — a very plausible 0x65. Crucially, a held mutex in a shared PRIV mutex block survives a SEC2-engine reset, which fits our data exactly (the poison survived v10's engine reset). That's why I asked the agent to analyze the mutex path as a prime suspect alongside the AON scratch.```

author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```The "5 PLMs". In the current proven recipe it's actually 4 FB-geometry PLMs + LMR + reset-PLM-last = 6 writes (fits the SEC2 DMA buffer's 6-slot budget):  0x9A0148, 0x9A014C, 0x9A0008, 0x9A000C — the 4 FBPA PLMs 0x100CE0 (LMR), 0x8403C4 (reset-PLM, written last = 0xff) The 5th PLM was 0x100b10 (the PFB master PLM) — that's the "5 PLMs + LMR + reset = 7" that overflowed the 6-write budget. We then proved 0x100b10 is unnecessary (LMR writes at PL3 and per-FBPA CFG1 lands with just the 4 FBPA PLMs open), so we dropped it → 4 PLMs → 6 writes → fits. And yes: these are all FB-geometry PLMs — zero compute PLMs touched. The compute cluster (SS0/SS1 0x82381C/823820, feature-override 0x823804) is completely untouched for the memory unlock.```

PL3/HS-only registers → must go through the HS ROP (the exploit's HS gadget). That's LMR at PL3, the AON scratch 0x1182d0 (PL0 read = 0xbadf5108), and opening the FB-PLMs themselves. ````

author: bigptoughneigh
message: ```What ***__must__*** go through the driver. Only one thing, really: booting GSP-RM (the booter-load + RISC-V bootstrap that kgspBootstrap orchestrates) and thereby exposing the device to CUDA/userspace. The memory unlock itself needs no driver at all — it's all BAR0 + one HS LMR write. But a CUDA-usable 40GB deliverable requires a booted GSP-RM, and that boot is the 0x65 we're stuck on. Everything the driver does around it (WprMeta population, FWSEC invocation, booter load) is just register/DMA sequences that in principle could be driven from BAR0/ROP — the driver is only the convenient orchestrator. So nothing is fundamentally driver-locked except the fact that CUDA needs a live GSP-RM.```

author: petrikrohn_26497
message: > Their 16-bit truncation is the root cause of their STRAP/LMR failure. The indirect engine truncates 32-bit addresses to 16 bits, so their writes to 0x9A0204, 0x100CE0, 0x823804, and 0x1FA824 go to wrong offsets (0x0204, 0x0CE0, 0x3804, 0xA824 — all BADF values). They need to use direct Falcon register writes (not the indirect engine) to reach the full 24-bit BAR0 address space.  No! This has been confirmed multiple times: The BAR0 writes go through to the correct address and are readable from the host. If they survive FLR is another sssue.  > FWSEC resets geometry — the VBIOS devinit ucode reads the VBIOS strap (0x44=10GB) and sets all three registers to 10GB during kgspPrepareForBootstrap. The geometry must be re-set AFTER FWSEC.  This is questionable, but is trivially easy to test. Write the memory geometry using <@532035649700626453>'s scripts. Check that the writes go through by reading the registers from the host. Do a FLR reset. Read the values again and check.  You must do the above steps yourself. Do not let some clanker do it for you. In fact this should have been done a week ago, but the clankers here were too stupid to do it!   > FBPA PLMs at 0x9A0148, 0x9A014C, 0x9A0008, 0x9A000C are 0xFF after FLR but become 0xFFFFFF8F after GSP-RM boot (bits 4,6 HS-locked).  No! Do not fool around with the FBPAs. They are set by CFG1. It is the only register you need to write.  > Compute PLM (0x823804), SS0 (0x82381C), SS1 (0x823820) are all PL0-writable — we confirmed this directly. The compute unlock works from the host without HS code.  No! Only SS0 and SS1 are writable from the host. The compute PLM must be set by the Falcon in HS mode.  If this was not so, any Nvidia card could be "unlocked" without any exploit.
